We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. For businesses and developers, that means frontier performance at costs that make sense at scale.

GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new quality bar for AI in complex professional work. Its slides, spreadsheets, and documents read less like AI, and more closely follow the templates you provide and the conventions of your field. signals.excerpt:
Published: November 17, 2026 | Authors: Andrew Barba, Shar Dara, Casey Gowrie, Colton Padden, Rui Conti, Ben Pankow, Owen Kephart, Murat Sutunc, Chad Hietala | Category: Company News

---

Today we're announcing eve 1.0, the open-source framework for building production-ready agents.

Since the public preview in June, we've worked with early adopters to prepare eve for 1.0, shipping 230+ releases and merging thousands of pull requests. With this release, eve is now generally available.

We've made eve faster, expanded integrations, and improved observability. Security controls let you decide which actions need approval and what data gets collected. We've also made it easier for coding agents to build with, measuring that experience with a rigorous evaluation suite.

With eve handling your harness and infrastructure, you and your agent can focus on building instead.

## Build production agents on a harness you own

The harness in eve is the loop that calls models, runs tools, and delegates work to subagents. You choose the model, add or replace tools, edit instructions, and decide which actions need approval. The open-source Workflow SDK saves progress as the agent runs, so it can pick up from its last completed step after a crash. Multiplayer sessions and agent-to-agent calls are built in.

For managed hosting, deploy your eve agent to Vercel. Vercel Workflows handles durable execution, and Vercel Sandbox runs agent-generated code in isolation.

Build software factories that turn requests into tested pull requests, company brains that answer questions from your business data, or customer-facing agents in your product.

...

## Give agents memory across sessions

We added native memory so agents can carry context from one session to the next. You choose the memory's scope and can use the built-in file memory, a memory provider, or one you build yourself.

Built-in `fileMemory` keeps data in memory in `eve dev` and in a private Vercel Blob store you configure on Vercel.

Other providers include claude-mem, Hindsight, Kybernesis Arcana, Memanto, memco, Supermemory, and Upstash AgentKit.

...

signals.title: Tencent Launches Hy4 flash to Power High-Speed, Cost-Efficient AI Deployment for Everyday Workflows - Tencent
signals.excerpt:
November 16, 2026

Tencent today announced the release of Hy4 flash, the latest addition to its Hy model family. Hy4 flash has 224 billion total parameters (including 64 billion Engram parameters) with only 12 billion active parameters, and supports multimodal inputs and a context length of up to 1M tokens. It is the most cost-effective Hy model to date, priced at approximately US$0.070 per million input tokens, US$0.281 per million output tokens, and US$0.003 per million cached input tokens — a substantial reduction from Hy4.

Hy4 flash vs Hy4 API Price Comparison in USD (https://hy.tencent.ai/research/hy4-flash)

To achieve this level of cost performance while maintaining strong intelligence and practical utility, the Tencent Hy team made a series of engineering choices across the model pipeline:

- Pre-training: Hy4 flash incorporates hybrid attention, LatentMoE, and Engram architectural features. The KV cache size is just 1/24 that of Hy3 and 1/6 that of Hy4. Extensive scaling ladder experiments were conducted to ensure performance met expectations.
- Post-training: Drawing directly from Hy4’s architecture, the model inherits strong general intelligence. Reinforcement learning cuts average end-to-end task output tokens by 50 percent.
- Evaluation: The team built WorkIndex, an internal benchmark based on typical WorkBuddy tasks, paired with human evaluations, focusing on deliverable quality, single-turn output length, and task turnaround time rather than public benchmark scores detached from everyday work.
- Inference: Combining optimization using megakernel, 4-bit quantization, and DFly techniques, Hy4 flash achieves decoding speeds exceeding 150 tokens per second, enabling low-cost deployment at scale.

As a result, Hy4 flash slightly outperforms the larger Hy4 Preview (770 billion total parameters, 49 billion active parameters) in overall effectiveness, at a significantly lower cost. Based on the internal WorkIndex benchmark, which covers PowerPoint deck creation and editing, document editing, spreadsheet repair, audio/video processing, and visual understanding tasks typical of use with WorkBuddy — Hy4 flash delivers a per-task cost of just 1/13 that of Hy4 Preview, 1/20 that of Hy4, and 1/8 that of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (Max tier, peak-hour pricing).

signals.title: Introducing the Microsoft Copilot SDK 2.0
signals.excerpt:
2026.11.17

Today at Ignite, we’re announcing the new Microsoft Copilot SDK (previously named GitHub Copilot SDK). It gives you direct, programmatic access to the Microsoft Copilot harness powering products across our entire portfolio for coding, non-coding, and creative apps, platforms, and services. It can be used to build agents that run anywhere and can use any inference.

...

### A shared, multi-tenanted runtime 

The first big change in 2.0 is a runtime that can host many sessions within a single process. Each session has its own state, credentials, tools, files, and history. No session can see another. Sessions become cheap and highly disposable. Creating one doesn’t need to start a container, a process, or a VM, which cuts both time to first token and operating cost. When users ask a simple question, the runtime can respond immediately with performant inference. 

That only works if the runtime itself is lean, so we rebuilt it in Rust. On the same warmed workload, creating a client and a session and completing one turn went from 5.25 seconds on the TypeScript CLI to 55.3 milliseconds with the Rust core in-process. Scalability improved as well: 10 clients now use 126 MB of memory instead of 1,383 MB, and throughput rose from 7.55 to 120 sessions per second.

signals.title: SID AI Releases SID-2 Agentic Search Model With 0.720 NDCG Swarm Mode - MarkTechPost
signals.excerpt:
By

Michal Sutter

November 17, 2026

SID AI has released SID-2, its second-generation agentic search model, alongside SID-2 Swarm. SID-2 is an agentic search model from SID AI that searches your data, reads results and returns ranked document IDs. It replaces fixed RAG pipelines with a model that decides what to search next. 

## TL;DR

- Size: Context window is 262k tokens per the report (256k on sid.ai/models).
- Runs on: Hosted API at platform.sid.ai, plus Baseten and SageMaker reference paths. SID’s latency figures assume 1 B200 GPU at 8 concurrent queries.
- Performance: A single agent matches Claude Opus 5.5 on retrieval quality. Swarms beat every model SID tested.
- Best: SID-2 Swarm (12 agents) scores 0.720 NDCG, above GPT-6 Astra at 0.704.
- Worst: SID-2 Low scores 0.556 NDCG, 0.148 below GPT-6 Astra. Astra still leads on California law, SEC filings and FiQA.
- Bottom line: Best: frontier-level retrieval at a fraction of the latency. Worst: no disclosed size, weights or independent evals yet.

## What is SID-2 and how does it work?

SID-2 is a small search specialist, not a general chat model. A static pipeline runs rewrite, embed, search and rerank in a fixed order. SID-2 instead searches, reads results, adapts and searches again.

Developers implement the search tools against their own backend. A `text_search` tool covers keyword search and a `search` tool covers vector search. The model ends each episode by calling `report_helpful_ids` with a ranked list. No reindexing or data movement is required, since SID-2 only sees what your tools return.

SID-2 Swarm runs several agents that message each other and fork their context into new agents. Each agent explores a separate slice of the corpus. SID argues search gains more from reading more documents than from reasoning harder about each one.

### What are reasoning effort and Metric Steering?

SID-2 offers low, medium and high reasoning effort. Each level was trained as a separate expert, then merged with multi-teacher on-policy distillation. Metric Steering lets users target NDCG, F1 or Recall@k, with k from 1 to 50. On SID’s 506-question validation set, SID-2 at high effort scores 0.14 to 0.22 higher per metric than the base model.

...

## How does SID-2 perform on benchmarks?

SID built a 506-question benchmark across 19 corpora. These include HotpotQA, Enron emails, SEC filings, PubMed and BrowseComp-Plus. All numbers below are self-reported from Tables 2 to 4 of the report.

- SID-2 Medium: 0.585 NDCG in 3.11 s, versus Claude Opus 5.5 (medium) at 0.577 in 25.1 s.
- SID-2 Swarm, 6 agents: 0.701 NDCG in 17.7 s, versus GPT-6 Astra (max) at 0.704 in 135 s.
- SID-2 Swarm, 12 agents: 0.720 NDCG, the highest score in the table.
- Baselines: BM25 scores 0.260 and vector search plus reranker scores 0.287.

Swarm leads on 11 of 19 corpora. On WixQA, a single high-effort agent matches Astra at about 232x lower cost. At its lowest effort, SID-2 beats 4 parallel SID-1 runs with 13x fewer FLOPs.

## SID-2 vs GPT-6 Astra vs Claude Opus 5.5

| Feature | SID-2 (medium) | SID-2 Swarm (6 agents) | GPT-6 Astra (max) | Claude Opus 5.5 (medium) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Agentic search model | Multi-agent search | General LLM | General LLM |
| Parameters | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Not disclosed |
| Context | 262k (report) / 256k (site) | Effectively infinite (per SID) | Not disclosed | 1M |
| NDCG, SID benchmark | 0.585 | 0.701 | 0.704 | 0.577 |
| Inference time per query | 3.11 s | 17.7 s | 135 s | 25.1 s |
| Cost per 1,000 queries | $6.54 | $263 | $2,141 | $131 |
| API price (input / output per 1M) | $0.25 / $1.00 | $0.50 / $2.00 | $10 / $50 | $4 / $20 |

NDCG, time and cost rows are measured by SID on its own benchmark. Retrieval backend time is excluded.

## How can developers deploy SID-2?

SID-2 is available through SID’s API and on Baseten. SDKs exist for Python (`sid-sdk`), TypeScript (`@sid-ai/sid-sdk`) and Go (`github.com/sidhq/sid-go`). A SageMaker helper covers AWS deployments. The reference implementation uses the OpenAI client format.

SID-2 costs $0.25 per million input tokens and $1.00 per million output tokens. Swarm costs $0.50 and $2.00. Cached input is 10% of the input price.

Organization

Hugging Face says it describes CQ, a calibration-free quantization format, and GCMP, a parameter-efficient adapter positioned as a replacement for LoRA. The material is dated November 14, 2026.

Hugging Face says CQ needs no calibration data. Its input is a Hugging Face checkpoint, and it runs layer by layer. The post says GCMP is compatible with CQ, NF4 and full-precision bases.

Hugging Face lists the CQ model at 18 GB and the NF4 model at 22.4 GB.

The benchmark model is Qwen3.8-27B. In company-reported results, the CQ base scores 0.65 on GSM8K. Hugging Face says CQ shows no significant difference from BF16 across all benchmarks. It reports an NF4 loss of 12.0 points on GSM8K against BF16. Hugging Face gives the benchmark size as 200–1,140 questions per task.

The post reports mean KL divergence on WikiText-2 of 0.0282 for CQ against BF16, and 0.033 for NF4 against BF16.

On Qwen3.8-27B, GCMP has 2.9M parameters, and its adapter is about 11 MB on disk. LoRA at rank thirty-two has about 159M trainable parameters and occupies about 320 MB on disk.

The adapter runs used the Alpaca dataset and a fixed set of training settings, covering steps, batch size, sequence length, learning rate and random seed. Hugging Face says those settings were identical across the compared runs.

Hugging Face reports that, on an NF4 base, GCMP scored 4.0 points higher on GSM8K (p = 0.04) than LoRA.

On ARC-Challenge, Hugging Face reports that CQ with GCMP was lower on ARC-Challenge (−4.2, p = 0.001) than NF4 with GCMP.

Hugging Face says the CQ + LoRA run is still in progress. The first CQ + LoRA adapter it evaluated came from an older trainer version, which the post describes as broken.

Hugging Face reports that CQ trainer step time fell from 27.6 seconds per step before a recent improvement to 8.6 seconds now.

Hugging Face says vLLM serving of GCMP currently requires a CQ base, while GCMP adapters on full-precision models run in Transformers for now. CQ supports pipeline parallelism across GPUs, but tensor parallelism is not yet supported. The post gives a per-token adapter routing buffer in vLLM of ~1 MB.

The CUDA kernels ship compiled. Hugging Face says they include a license check and are free during early access.

By Sergey Kostenchuk Published 2026-11-16 Updated 2026-11-17

...

Baseten has released deepseek-ultrafast, an open-source inference engine—responsible for real-time language model response generation—written in Rust and CUDA ... The DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-Fast model is already available via Baseten's OpenAI-compatible API, and the open code allows teams with suitable hardware to independently reproduce the claimed benchmarks.

### What happened

Baseten published the basetenlabs/deepseek-ultrafast repository containing a Rust and CUDA engine written for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, targeting NVIDIA B200 and B300 GPUs with sm_100a and sm_103a architectures. According to the README, decoding reaches 2060 tokens per second on a setup of eight B300s in a TP8 configuration: one step takes 2.71 milliseconds with an average accepted block length of 5.6 tokens, while 1740 tokens per second are claimed on four GB300 accelerators. Prefilling one million tokens fits within 11.7 seconds, equivalent to 85,000 tokens per second. The engine supports a 1-million-token context and can share the KV-cache across multiple servers via Redis and RDMA. According to the authors, GPU kernels were refined by coding agents working with FlashInfer and SGLang sources, and the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-Fast model is delivered to clients via Baseten Model APIs through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint inference.baseten.co.

...

### What is currently unknown / limitations

All key figures are taken from Baseten's own README and refer to the batch=1 mode after warm-up: there are no independent public replications or detailed measurement methodologies yet, so the metrics should be treated as a hypothesis subject to verification. Due to speculative decoding, the actual speed will depend on the proportion of accepted draft tokens for a specific model and load. Direct comparison with Cerebras and Groq is incorrect: this is a measurement of single-stream latency for a single request versus metrics from specialized accelerators obtained on other models and methodologies. The engine only runs on sm_100a and sm_103a architectures, i.e., on B200, B300, and GB300, and will not work on other hardware. Finally, the thesis about recursive self-improvement remains the post author's interpretation, not an established fact: humans are still participating in the optimization loop.

signals.title: Neo4j releases Relate, an open source in-memory database built for AI agents
signals.excerpt:
Mon 16 Nov 2026 · First reported by Cyprus Shipping News

...

## The short version

- Relate is open source under the Apache 2.0 license and built in Rust
- It runs in-process, in memory, with optional disk storage for durability
- It includes an MCP server, a command-line tool, and Bolt and HTTP query endpoints
- Errors carry retryable flags, and a row cap stops large results from flooding an agent
- Neo4j cites Gartner: machine users reach 75% of database workloads by 2029

...

## What Neo4j released

Neo4j, a company that makes graph databases, has released Relate. A graph database stores information as things and the connections between them, which suits questions like "who is linked to whom, and through what." As Cyprus Shipping News reported, Relate is open source, written in the Rust programming language, and aimed at AI agents and the systems built around them.

The headline claim is speed of setup. Neo4j says a coding agent, meaning an AI that writes and runs code on its own, can create a database and begin building an application in milliseconds. The announcement also says it installs quickly and runs anywhere.

One caveat up front: the article is based on a company release, distributed through Business Wire. The performance figures are the vendor's own, and the source gives no independent benchmarks or pricing details.

## In memory and in process

Two terms explain the design. In-memory means the data lives in the computer's fast working memory instead of being fetched from disk each time. In-process embedded means the database runs inside the same program as the agent, so there is no separate database server to set up or connect to.

Neo4j says reads in memory take under a millisecond, which matters because agents tend to read and write constantly as they work through a task. Memory is lost when a machine restarts, so Relate offers protection. A write-ahead log, a running record of changes written to disk before they are applied, can be switched on for durable stores, and the database can also flush its state to disk for long-term storage.

...

## Features aimed at agent habits

Most of the announcement is about small design choices that reflect how agents fail and recover. Relate detects when an agent harness, the software wrapper that runs an agent, is calling it. When something goes wrong, it returns structured errors with an explicit flag saying whether retrying makes sense. Neo4j says this lets an agent correct itself without custom code to interpret error text.

Another choice limits how much comes back. Relate caps the number of rows in a result and adds a marker showing the result was cut short. The point is to avoid overfilling an agent's context window, the limited amount of text a model can consider at once. Agents then receive results of a predictable size.

Connectivity comes built in. Relate has a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, a common standard for letting agents use outside tools, plus a command-line tool. It also exposes Bolt and HTTP Query API v2 endpoints, so existing graph drivers, orchestration frameworks and developer tools should work with it.

## Graph queries and retrieval

Relate supports Cypher, the query language Neo4j uses for graph data. A single Cypher statement can search by vector similarity, which finds items with similar meaning, and follow connections through the graph in the same step. Neo4j says this supports multi-hop reasoning, where an answer depends on following several links in a row, and GraphRAG, which feeds a model facts drawn from a graph. The company says this gives agents more accurate results and fewer hallucinations, meaning invented answers. That claim is Neo4j's and is not tested in the source.

The release says Relate is 100% openCypher compliant and more than 97% compliant with GQL, the standard graph query language. Those numbers suggest queries written for other graph systems may carry over, though the source does not say how that was measured. It is released under the Apache 2.0 license, a permissive open source license.

Building on the Preview version’s exploration of parameter efficiency, the model reuses layer parameters through a Loop structure and incorporates manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC) to extend computational depth with approximately 9B parameters, supporting complex reasoning, coding, tool use and multimodal tasks. Thanks to its efficient looping architecture, the official 4-bit quantized weights occupy only about 4.9GB, with deployment GPU memory requirements as low as under 10GB. This significantly broadens the range of compatible hardware, making it possible for chips with limited GPU memory to deliver performance comparable to leading 27B-class models.

Since the Preview release, we have received considerable community interest and feedback on model usage, inference deployment and ecosystem integration. The official release retains the Loop and dual-stream mHC architecture, further improves performance on agent, coding and data analysis tasks, and continues to explore how looped computation can enhance model capabilities.

SenseNova Loop-9B has approximately 9B parameters in total. By executing shared intermediate layers twice, it expands 32 physical decoder layers into 56 layer computations. The model accepts text and image inputs, produces text outputs, and supports a context length of up to 512K tokens. In agent and data analysis evaluations, it demonstrates competitiveness comparable to Qwen3.8-27B: its NL2Repo score of 41.36 approaches Qwen3.8-27B’s 44.60, while its AIDABench score of 65.31 exceeds the latter’s 65.01.

- Shared loop module: Layers 4–27 form a weight-sharing loop module that runs twice, enabling 56 decoder-layer computations in a single forward pass.
- Dual-stream mHC: Learnable mappings route and fuse information across two residual streams within the loop module.
- Hybrid attention: The decoder uses groups of four layers, combining three linear-attention layers with one full-attention layer.
- Long-context multimodality: The training regimen covers text, images, code and tool-use trajectories, extending context length to up to 512K tokens.
- Resource-efficient on-premises deployment: With 4-bit weight quantization and an 8-bit KV cache, inference at a 256K context length requires approximately 15 GiB of GPU memory, lowering the barrier to local and on-premises deployment.
- Official quantization available on day zero: An official AWQ 4-bit quantized version is available from launch day for rapid deployment.

SenseNova Loop-9B model weights and related code are now available for developers and researchers to download, deploy and explore.

signals.title: Context API extracts full context from any web page
signals.excerpt:
2026. nov. 17.

...

When someone asks a chatbot a question, an AI agent may need to read several web pages to answer it. Standard search results often return only snippets. Fetching a page directly can return raw HTML, which is full of navigation, cookie banners, and ads. Agents need the page’s context in a format a model can use, while developers need a way to control how fresh that context must be.

Today we’re launching the Perplexity Context API, which reads up to 10 URLs and returns clean markdown, HTML, links, and query-based snippets for each page. The information comes from Perplexity's vast web index or a live fetch. Agents can specify the freshness of each request, and validate the source of each result.

## Context API supports a variety of formats

Agents can initiate a request by providing a list of URLs and specifying the output formats. The API returns a result for each URL in the same order.

Context API supports a variety of response formats:

- Markdown: The page content as clean Markdown, ready to place in a model’s context.
- HTML: The page's HTML, for applications that run their own parsing.
- Links: The links on the page as absolute URLs, without duplicates and in page order so an agent can decide where to go next.
- Snippets: The passages of the page most relevant to a query provided, within the token limit set by the developer for each page.

Context API selects passages from each page that are relevant to the query, rather than generating a summary. As a result, the model receives the page’s original wording, but only the selected passages, so there is less text to process.

Every successful result also includes metadata such as the title, description, language, author, and published date, plus the page's Open Graph tags. To build the Markdown, the Context API splits a page into blocks and a model scores each block as main content or boilerplate. Only the content blocks are kept.

...

## Control freshness and handle URLs reliably

By default, the Context API first checks Perplexity’s web index for a copy of the page fetched within the last two days. If there isn't one, it fetches the page live. Developers can change `max_age_seconds` to `0` to always read the live pages, for prices, scores, and breaking news. For reference material that rarely changes, they can raise it. Set `cache_only` to true for workloads that should never trigger a live request.

Each result records whether the content came from a stored copy or a live fetch, and when it was fetched.

URLs in a request are fetched in parallel, each with its own time budget and its own status. One slow or broken page doesn’t fail the others. The status indicates what happened with each URL, so an agent can retry only the pages that timed out and keep the rest.

## Context API returns usable, complete content

We tested the Context API against Firecrawl, Exa, Parallel, Keenable and Context.dev on 1,000 URLs sampled from real agent fetch requests. The set covers 715 sites and includes government and academic sources and non-English pages. A separate judge model then scored the outputs without knowing which provider produced each one.

The chart measures performance on three criteria:

- Usable: The share of URLs that came back with the page's real content, not an error page or an empty result.
- Fact recall: The judge collects the key facts found on a page across all providers, then checks which of them each output contains. A failed fetch scores zero.
- Content precision: The share of returned text that is page content, not cookie notices, navigation, or ads, averaged over all URLs. A failed fetch scores zero.

In this evaluation the Context API returned usable content for 92.3% of URLs, recovered 87.9% of the key facts, and demonstrated 80.3% precision.

## Pricing

Context API costs $1 per 1,000 URLs fetched. Developers pay for each URL that returns ok. URLs that fail aren’t billed.

signals.title: New Research Challenges GPU Utilization as Measure of Inference Infrastructure
signals.excerpt:
Nov 16, 2026, 09:00 ET

New NAND Research report underscores that busy GPUs aren't an accurate measure of productive output; introduces new Inference Economics Scorecard to measure inference infrastructure by the useful work it delivers, as applied in an eight-hour benchmark with Nebius on NVIDIA HGX B300 GPUs and WEKA NeuralMesh.

CHICAGO, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- From Supercomputing 2026: WEKA, the AI data and memory infrastructure company, in collaboration with market intelligence firm NAND Research, today introduced the Inference Economics Scorecard, a new common framework for measuring inference infrastructure productivity and economic value by the useful work it delivers rather than by how busy it keeps GPUs. The scorecard defines nine measures, including tokens per watt, cost per inference, and context retention. It sets four testing rules, including runs of at least eight hours and counting only successful output. Already applied in a benchmark with Nebius, the AI cloud company, it comes as inference is claiming a growing share of AI infrastructure spending and buyers hit power, memory, and rack-space limits.

...

Why GPU Utilization Falls Short for Inference

For years, training was the dominant AI workload. Because training keeps GPUs busy with large, predictable jobs, GPU utilization became the default measure of AI infrastructure productivity. Inference, especially agentic inference, places very different demands on GPUs. An agent does not simply answer a prompt; it completes a task over many steps, and at each step it re-reads the context it built earlier. After the GPU evicts that context from memory to make room for other users and sessions, it must recompute it when the task returns, and the task makes no further progress until that work is done. The result is a GPU that is fully utilized but unproductive because it wastes cycles recomputing the same tokens multiple times.

The Inference Economics Scorecard measures inference systems at production scale: completed requests across many concurrent users, sustained over hours rather than minutes.

...

From Busy to Productive: How the Scorecard Works The Inference Economics Scorecard defines nine measures of inference performance and economics: tokens per watt, tokens per rack, cost per inference, GPU goodput, time to first token and end-to-end latency, memory efficiency, operational density, agent concurrency, and context retention. It also sets the discipline for testing against them:

- The same workload and service targets across every system tested
- Measurement of the whole serving stack
- Runs of at least eight hours
- Only successful output counted

"The most expensive mistake in AI infrastructure right now is buying for peak throughput and paying for repeated work," said Steve McDowell, principal analyst and founder at NAND Research. ... We designed the scorecard so buyers can hold any system to the ... The Nebius benchmark shows what that discipline reveals, because it ran for the full eight hours and counted every request that failed or timed out."

Putting It to the Test: Real Agent Load, Sustained for Eight Hours WEKA and Nebius recently applied the scorecard's rules in a joint benchmark on NVIDIA HGX B300 systems and reported results on several measures. The test ran on one eight-GPU node serving DeepSeek-V4-Pro to 512 active sessions drawn from a corpus of more than 5,000 real agentic coding sessions over eight hours per configuration, counting every failed and timed-out request.

Using WEKA NeuralMesh with Augmented Memory Grid, which pools NVMe across the cluster as a shared context tier, the node produced 3.7x the output tokens per GPU-hour compared with HBM-only serving on the same GPUs, and 97% of successfully completed requests reached a first token within five seconds, up from 44%. On HBM-only serving, 60% of prefill work was recomputed from context the cluster had already processed earlier in the session; with Augmented Memory Grid, 6.8%. At the measured rate, the HBM-only node would need about 30 hours to produce what Augmented Memory Grid produced in eight. The full benchmark is published at weka.io and nebius.com blogs.

...

Reproducible by Design: Open Traces and Tooling The traces and tooling behind the benchmark are open-sourced so anyone can run the same workload on their own systems and compare results on equal terms. Because the traces come from real agentic coding sessions rather than synthetic load, and include the varied timing and complexity of real work, they give any team a realistic stand-in for production.

signals.title: Co-Designing Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Inference | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
Agentic workloads, long documents, and large codebases are pushing context lengths from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds of thousands. At those lengths, attention becomes the most expensive part of a transformer layer. Dense attention scores every query against every key, so its cost per query grows with the context length N, and at 128K tokens it can take most of the prefill time in a layer.

The model-level solution is sparse attention, a transformer technique in which each query attends to only a small subset of the context, chosen per query, instead of all of it. This cuts both the compute and the memory traffic of attention on long context.

This post is a practical primer for model developers designing sparse attention that runs well on NVIDIA GPUs. It focuses on model-level sparse attention, where sparsity is trained into the model, rather than drop-in methods applied after training such as BLASST, MInference, or Quest. A production FP8 kernel is used to sweep the indexer’s design knobs (query heads, key heads, head dimension, compression ratio, and speculative-decoding depth), measure how Top-k cost scales, and compare token-level with block-level core attention.

Each section explains what the hardware rewards and why, and ends with a guideline you can apply to your own design. This post follows the same co-design approach as the earlier posts on dense attention and hardware-friendly LLM design.

signals.title: Qwen3.8 Flash Next NVFP4 QAD: NVIDIA ModelOpt | explainx.ai Blog
signals.excerpt:
Nvidia uploaded Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4-QAD on Nov 17, 2026—a 180B image-text MoE with aggressive ModelOpt QAD mixing NVFP4 and MXFP8. How it differs from NVFP4.

Nov 17, 2026· 8 min read· Yash Thakker

NVIDIA on November 17, 2026 added a second public quantization experiment atop Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4-QAD`, an image-text-to-text mixture-of-experts checkpoint exported with ModelOpt QAD after 100 optimizer updates. It ships the full multimodal stack— vision encoder, PLE n-gram embedding, and MTP module—in roughly 129.7 GB of safetensors shards.

For local inference engineers, the important distinction is naming: -QAD means quantization-aware training tweaks, not merely re-labeled NVFP4 weights. NVIDIA''s card warns the recipe is more aggressive than `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` and that accuracy gains are not statistically established.

## TL;DR

| Item | Model card claim |
| --- | --- |
| Base model | Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next |
| Training stack | NVIDIA ModelOpt + NeMo AutoModel (FSDP2) |
| QAD steps | 100 optimizer updates |
| Expert precision | NVFP4 routed + shared experts (trained) |
| Extra layers | GDN / QSA / indexer projections → MXFP8 |
| Disk footprint | ~129.7 GB weights |
| HF task | image-text-to-text |

## What QAD changes in the weight stack

A model core split into matching shards for distribution, echoing consolidated NVFP4 and MXFP8 safetensors

The Hugging Face README includes a component table. Summarized:

- Main LM routed experts (48 MoE groups) stay NVFP4 block size 16, trained with QAD.
- Shared experts (144 linear matrices) move to NVFP4 under QAD—where the earlier NVFP4-only release left them differently.
- GDN projections (180 matrices) use MXFP8 blocks under QAD.

NVIDIA explicitly says the repository name''s -QAD suffix identifies the method, not a promise that the old NVFP4 recipe stayed intact.

Consolidation note: NVIDIA merged shards for distribution, verified SHA256 against export, and claims tensor names, shapes, dtypes, and values are unchanged—relevant if you diff against internal checkpoints.
